planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Fatshedera is a bigeneric hybrid between Fatsia japonica and English ivy and inherits a sprawling, semi-vining habit that benefits from staking or a support if grown upright.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind. This unusual bigeneric cross between Fatsia japonica and English ivy was first raised in France in 1912 and combines the bold, glossy, lobed foliage of Fatsia with a looser, semi-climbing habit inherited from its ivy parent. Left unstaked it sprawls and roots where it touches soil, making a good shade groundcover or informal hedge, or it can be tied to a support for a more upright accent. It tolerates deep shade better than most broadleaf evergreens, is easy from cuttings, and needs only an occasional light pruning to control its size.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; Hummingbird is a compact, spreading selection of native summersweet that stays smaller than the species and tolerates wet soil well.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to shade; Hummingbird is a naturally dwarf, spreading selection of the native Southeastern shrub summersweet, staying compact and dense where the wild species can grow considerably taller. In mid-to-late summer it produces upright spikes of small, intensely fragrant white flowers that draw bees and butterflies in large numbers, followed by attractive seed capsules that persist into winter. It spreads slowly by suckers to form a low colony over time, tolerates wet, poorly drained sites better than most shrubs, and is one of the more reliable flowering shrubs for shady, damp corners of the garden.

common_name: El Dorado Nectarine (Genetic Dwarf Low-Chill Nectarine)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; El Dorado is a genetic dwarf that tops out at a fraction of standard tree size, making it well suited to containers and small gardens, with a low chill requirement good for zone 8-9.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; bred by Floyd Zaiger, El Dorado is a genetic dwarf nectarine that naturally grows to only six to eight feet, a fraction of a standard tree's size, while still producing full-sized, richly flavored yellow-fleshed fruit. Its low chill requirement of around 300 hours lets it fruit reliably in mild-winter regions like the Gulf South where standard nectarines often fail to break dormancy evenly. The compact size makes it an excellent choice for large containers or small yards, though the dense, naturally rounded canopy still benefits from light annual thinning to let light into the interior. Fruit ripens in early summer and is self-fruitful, requiring no separate pollinator.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Panamint has a low chill requirement well suited to zone 8-9 and produces reliably where standard nectarines struggle to break dormancy.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Panamint is a low-chill freestone nectarine developed for mild-winter growing regions, producing medium-to-large, richly flavored yellow-fleshed fruit with a sweet-tart balance typical of good dessert nectarines. Its comparatively low chilling requirement lets it flower and fruit reliably in areas like the Gulf South and lower South where standard high-chill nectarines fail to leaf out and bloom evenly. The tree is self-fruitful and ripens in early-to-mid summer; thin fruit to four to six inches apart along the branch in years of heavy set to improve size and reduce limb strain.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Bonanza is a genetic dwarf that stays compact enough for a large container or small patio bed, though its early bloom means it should be sited where late frosts are less likely to damage the flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun. Bonanza is a genetic dwarf apricot that naturally stays under six feet tall while still producing normal-sized, sweet, orange-fleshed fruit, making it one of the few apricots practical for a large container or a very small yard. Like most apricots it blooms quite early in spring, so a sheltered site away from low-lying frost pockets improves the odds of a good fruit set. The dense, compact form needs little pruning to maintain shape beyond removing crossing branches, and the tree is self-fruitful, requiring no separate pollinator variety.
